title: Operation Circle: How Gorazde Held
sources: ICTY Karadzic Trial Judgment (IT-95-5/18-T), Gorazde and Drina Valley findings
ICTY Galic Trial Judgment (IT-98-29-T), context on enclave isolation
Balkan Battlegrounds Vol. I, Chapter on the Drina Valley campaigns of 1992
content:
Goražde sits on the Drina river in eastern Bosnia, a long industrial town hemmed in by steep wooded ridges. Before the war it was an unremarkable municipal seat, best known for the Pobjeda chemical works and a hydroelectric dam upstream. By the spring of 1992 it had become something else entirely: an island of Bosniak-held territory in a sea of Bosnian Serb military control, the southern hinge of an arc of besieged enclaves stretching north along the Drina through Žepa and Srebrenica.

Throughout April, May, and June of 1992, Yugoslav People's Army (JNA) units and the emerging Bosnian Serb Army (VRS) drove Bosniak civilians out of villages on Goražde's outskirts in operations that the ICTY would later document as part of the systematic ethnic cleansing of the Drina valley. Refugees streamed into the town, swelling its population and straining food, fuel, and medical supplies. The defenders of Goražde were initially a patchwork of local Territorial Defence units, MUP police, and improvised volunteer formations, poorly armed and operating without a unified command. By midsummer, however, these units had begun to coalesce into what would become the ARBiH 1st and 31st Drina Strike Brigades.

In August 1992, ARBiH commanders launched a coordinated counteroffensive — known in Bosniak sources as Operation Circle (Operacija Krug) — to push VRS positions back from the immediate approaches to the town and to recover several outlying settlements. The operation was modest by the standards of later war: a few thousand soldiers, no armor to speak of, an artillery park measured in tubes rather than batteries. What it achieved, however, was strategically decisive. Over several weeks of fighting along the eastern and southern perimeter, ARBiH units consolidated a defensible pocket roughly twenty kilometres across, anchored on the town itself and the river crossings.

The consequences of that consolidation reached well beyond the local battlefield. Goražde would remain under siege for the rest of the war — its population endured artillery fire, sniping, malnutrition, and acute shortages of medicine. But the pocket did not collapse. Where Srebrenica and Žepa would fall in July 1995, Goražde held. The 1994 NATO ultimatum that produced an exclusion zone around the town followed precisely the perimeter that Operation Circle had drawn two years earlier. The pocket's persistence kept VRS forces tied down on a front that they had expected to liquidate quickly, and it preserved a Bosniak presence in the upper Drina valley that the post-war Dayton settlement would formalise.

The Karadžić trial judgment, in its findings on the Drina valley, treated Goražde as a case in which Bosnian Serb leadership had set political and military objectives — the elimination of Bosniak presence in a corridor running south from Zvornik — that local outcomes failed to deliver. Goražde's defenders were not, in any organised sense, the recipients of outside aid in 1992. They were a population that armed itself with what it had and held a perimeter that could not, by the terms of the larger campaign, be permitted to hold. That it did is one of the inflection points of the war's military history.
